questions.question: What does independence of two events mean?
choices: One event's occurrence does not change the other's probability

questions.question: For independent events A and B, what is P(A and B)?
For mutually exclusive events A and B, what is P(A or B)?
Two fair coins are tossed independently. What is P(two heads)?
A fair die and fair coin are used independently. How many equally likely paired outcomes exist?
What are mutually exclusive events?
choices: Events that must have equal probabilities

questions.question: What is P(rolling 1 or 2 on one fair six-sided die)?
Why can drawing without replacement make successive draws dependent?
choices: The first draw changes the size of each object
The first draw changes the remaining contents
The original sample space must have no outcomes

questions.question: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. After drawing red without replacement, what is P(red on the next draw)?
The same bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. If the first ball is replaced and remixed, what is P(red next)?
What is the general addition rule for two events?
choices: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) + P(A and B)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

questions.question: Why is overlap subtracted in the general addition rule?
choices: It represents impossible outcomes in every case
It must equal zero for every pair
It changes all event probabilities to equal values
It was counted in both P(A) and P(B)

questions.question: Two independent events have probabilities 0.4 and 0.5. What is the probability both occur?
Two fair coins are tossed. What is P(at least one head)?
What is P(A given B) when P(B) > 0?
Two fair six-sided dice are rolled independently. What is P(a total of 7)?
A bag has 4 red and 1 blue ball. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is P(both red)?
Events A and B have probabilities 0.6 and 0.5, with overlap 0.2. What is P(A or B)?
A fair coin is tossed three times independently. What is P(exactly two heads)?
Two nonzero-probability events are mutually exclusive. Why are they not independent?
choices: Knowing one occurred makes the other's probability zero
